query: Which material can be used for enhance glass-forming ability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Minor additions of Yttrium (Y) to a base metallic-glass composition increase its glass-forming ability.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline metallic-glass alloy without Y doping.
generation.intervention: Doping the baseline alloy with up to 5 at% Y by arc melting and suction casting.
generation.conditions: Systematic variation of Y content (0–5 at%), controlled melt temperature (~1600 K), vacuum casting environment, characterized using XRD, DSC, and TEM.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized atomic rearrangements induced by Y additions.
generation.mechanism: Y doping induces structural frustration and reduces the propensity for crystal nucleation, leading to enhanced glass stability upon cooling.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in glass-forming ability (e.g., higher critical casting thickness) relative to the undoped alloy.
generation.baseline: Same base metallic-glass composition without Y doping, prepared under otherwise identical conditions.
generation.boundary: Excessive Y content (>5 at%) or different alloy compositions may negate or alter the GFA improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of GFA improvement remains unquantified without additional experimental data.

falsification_experiment.design: Melt and cast a control alloy and multiple test specimens, each with different Y additions up to 5 at%. Examine glass formation and crystallization behavior under the same cooling conditions.
measurements: Critical casting thickness of each sample
Onset temperatures for glass transition and crystallization via DSC
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped alloys do not exhibit a measurable increase in glass-forming ability (e.g., no change in critical casting thickness or crystallization resistance), the hypothesis is falsified.

chosen.lever: Minor additions of Yttrium (Y) to a base metallic-glass composition
